ai_summary: Great Britain is currently generating 13.6 GW of wind power, with estimated Scottish wind output reaching 5.0 GW, representing 49.5% of installed Scottish wind capacity. This robust clean generation drives Scottish carbon intensity down to 0 gCO2/kWh, contrasting sharply with the GB-wide level of 121 gCO2/kWh. However, transmission bottlenecks prevent this surplus renewable power from flowing southward to major demand centers, creating substantial operational friction. Consequently, Scottish generation curtailed so far today stands at 44690.3 MWh, accruing a constraint cost of about £1,135,763. Because this clean power could not be exported, balancing mechanisms required fossil generation to ramp up elsewhere on the network. It is estimated that 8491157.0 m3 of gas was burned elsewhere to replace it, adding 15641.6 tonnes CO2 into the atmosphere. This ongoing dynamic demonstrates the dual financial and environmental penalties caused by existing transmission limits. Until cross-border network capacity is reinforced, high-potential zero-carbon generation will continue to be restricted, shifting balancing costs onto consumers while forcing reliance on carbon-intensive thermal assets to meet system demand.
